cues.text: A Household Jesus Loved
In the small village of Bethany , just outside Jerusalem on the slope of the Mount of Olives, lived three siblings — Martha, Mary, and Lazarus .
The Gospel of John describes them simply and movingly: 'Jesus loved Martha, and her sister Mary, and Lazarus' (John 11:5).
Their home became one of the few places in the Gospels where Christ is shown enjoying ordinary friendship and hospitality, a household he visited repeatedly during his journeys to and from Jerusalem.
Martha's Service

St. Luke preserves the best-known scene of the sisters' contrasting temperaments: while Martha busied herself with the work of hosting Jesus and his disciples, her sister Mary sat quietly at his feet, listening to his teaching.
When Martha asked Jesus to tell Mary to help her, he answered gently that Mary 'has chosen the good portion,' without condemning Martha's own labor of hospitality.
The Church has long read this scene as balancing the active and contemplative life rather than favoring one over the other.
The Raising of Lazarus

The Gospel's most dramatic episode involving the family comes in John 11: when Lazarus fell gravely ill, the sisters sent word to Jesus, who delayed his arrival until Lazarus had already died and lay four days in the tomb.
Meeting the grieving Martha on the road, Jesus declared, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' drawing from her one of Scripture's most complete confessions of faith.
Then he went to the tomb and, in the presence of a gathered crowd, called Lazarus back to life.
A Family Under Threat

The stunning miracle of Lazarus's raising converted many onlookers to belief in Jesus, but it also hardened the resolve of the chief priests, who from that point began actively plotting Christ's death.
According to John's Gospel, they considered putting Lazarus himself to death as well, since so many were coming to faith because of him.
A Final Meal Together
Shortly before his Passion, Jesus returned to Bethany for a meal at which Martha again served and Lazarus sat among the guests.
Mary anointed Jesus's feet with costly perfume in an act of devotion that provoked criticism from Judas but drew Christ's own defense of her.
It was the last recorded scene of the family together in the Gospels.
Legacy
Scripture tells us nothing certain of the siblings' lives after these events, though later tradition, especially in the West, held that they traveled to Provence in southern France to evangelize.
This is a legend without solid historical foundation but reflected in the dedication of churches and shrines to them there.
Their shared feast preserves the memory of an ordinary household transformed by friendship with Christ.
It was a home of service, contemplation, grief, faith, and finally resurrection, offered to every believer as an image of what discipleship in daily life can look like.
